title: Hebrew spoken again
hookLine: Eliezer Ben-Yehuda helps revive Hebrew as a daily language

lines: A LANGUAGE FOR PRAYER AND BOOKS.
cards: Ask for an ice cream in Tel Aviv, a bus ticket in Haifa, a phone charger in Jerusalem, and you'll do it in Hebrew. It sounds ordinary. But for a long stretch of history, few people asked for bread in Hebrew.

They prayed in it, studied Torah and Talmud in it, and scholars wrote letters and poems in it across oceans. At the kitchen table, though, Jews spoke Yiddish, Ladino, Arabic, Persian, German, Russian.
Hebrew was for heaven and for books. Then a stubborn man in Jerusalem decided his kitchen would be different.

teach.b: He grew up in the Russian Empire, studied in Paris, and came to Jerusalem with one fixed idea: a people returning to its land should speak its own language there, every day, about everything. So he did it at home.
As the family story goes, he and his wife raised their son speaking only Hebrew, and he would not let other languages be spoken around the boy. Visitors found it strange.
Some religious neighbors were upset, because to them Hebrew was a holy tongue, not something for shopping lists.
But a daily language needs daily words, and the old books had no words for many things in a modern street or house.

So Ben-Yehuda published his own Hebrew newspapers, and spent his life on an enormous dictionary, collecting words from the Bible, the Mishnah and later writings, and proposing new ones where nothing old would do.

Here is the part the legend sometimes leaves out: he did not do it alone. Teachers in the new farming villages taught their classes in Hebrew. Children carried it home to parents who had come from everywhere.

teach.h: TEACHERS AND CHILDREN MADE IT STICK.
teach.b: Families, schools and writers made it stick. The prophet Zephaniah has a line about a day when God will turn to the peoples a pure language, so that all may call on God's name.
Ben-Yehuda's dream was more modest and more strange: a language of prayer, at last, used to ask someone to pass the salt.

how: Hebrew is the language of Jewish prayer and Torah study around the world, and in Israel it is also the everyday spoken language; Jews outside Israel may learn some Hebrew for prayer.

games.q: you are Ben-Yehuda. you need a word for something modern, and the Bible doesn't have one. what do you do?
o: search old Hebrew books, and coin a new word if nothing fits.
leave it out of the language.
games.why: his dictionary gathered words from the Bible, the Mishnah and later writings, and proposed new ones where nothing old would do.

practice: Try one Hebrew word: shalom, which means peace, and is also hello and goodbye, or todah, which means thank you. Say it once, quietly, out loud, and notice its shape in your mouth.
This word was in prayer books long before it was in shops; now it's in both.

wordCard.voice: Ben-Yehuda. The man who insisted his family, and then a people, speak Hebrew every day, from the kitchen table to the street, and spent his life writing a dictionary for it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: pass the salt, in Hebrew. Children carried it home, and it stayed. Same time tomorrow.
